pack.name: Professional communication
pack.description: Ten precise words for clear, thoughtful, and effective workplace communication.

items.meaning: Showing small but important differences in meaning, feeling, or opinion.
items.explanation: Use it when an idea, answer, or situation is more detailed and subtle than a simple yes-or-no description.
items.origin: From French nuance, meaning a slight shade or variation, ultimately related to Latin nubes: cloud.
examples: The report gives a nuanced view of the market.
Her nuanced answer acknowledged both sides of the issue.
The policy needs a more nuanced explanation.
He made a nuanced distinction between urgency and importance.
The conversation became more nuanced after we heard the customer feedback.

items.meaning: Giving a lot of information clearly in only a few words.
items.explanation: Use it to praise a message, summary, or explanation that is brief without leaving out what matters.
items.origin: From Latin concisus, meaning cut short or brief.
examples: Please keep the project update concise.
Her concise email answered every question.
The presenter gave a concise overview of the plan.
A concise subject line helps people find the message later.
He was concise but still polite during the meeting.

items.meaning: Truthful and direct, especially about something that may be difficult to say.
items.explanation: Use it for honest feedback or open conversation when directness is helpful and respectful.
items.origin: From Latin candidus, meaning white, bright, or sincere.
examples: She gave candid feedback on the proposal.
Let us have a candid conversation about the deadline.
His candid response helped us solve the problem faster.
The survey encouraged candid comments from employees.
Be candid, but make sure your feedback is constructive.

items.meaning: Careful and persistent in doing work or duties.
items.explanation: Use it to describe someone who works steadily, pays attention to responsibilities, and follows through.
items.origin: From Latin diligere, meaning to value, esteem, or take delight in.
examples: She is diligent about documenting each decision.
The diligent review caught an error before launch.
He made diligent efforts to understand the new process.
A diligent follow-up can build trust with clients.
The team was diligent in testing the update.

items.meaning: Able to change easily to suit new conditions or situations.
items.explanation: Use it for people, plans, or systems that respond well when circumstances change.
items.origin: From Latin adaptare, meaning to fit or adjust to.
examples: An adaptable team can handle changing priorities.
She stayed adaptable when the client changed the brief.
The software is adaptable to different business needs.
Being adaptable is useful in a fast-moving role.
Their adaptable process allowed the project to continue remotely.

items.meaning: Showing a deep and accurate understanding of a person, problem, or situation.
items.explanation: Use it to praise an observation, question, or analysis that reveals something important others may have missed.
items.origin: Formed from insight, meaning an inner sight or clear understanding.
examples: Her insightful question changed the direction of the discussion.
The interview contains several insightful comments about leadership.
He gave an insightful analysis of the customer data.
The mentor offered an insightful perspective on my career choice.
Your feedback was both kind and insightful.

items.meaning: Done consciously and intentionally, rather than by accident or without thought.
items.explanation: Use it for a careful choice, action, or process that has been planned with a clear purpose.
items.origin: From Latin deliberare, meaning to weigh or consider carefully.
examples: The change was deliberate, not an oversight.
She took a deliberate approach to building the new team.
We need to be deliberate about how we use customer data.
His deliberate pause gave everyone time to think.
The design uses deliberate spacing to make the page easier to read.

items.meaning: Able to be believed because it seems trustworthy and well supported.
items.explanation: Use it for evidence, sources, explanations, or people that deserve trust because they are reliable.
items.origin: From Latin credibilis, meaning worthy of belief, from credere: to believe.
examples: Use credible sources in the final report.
The explanation is credible because the data supports it.
She built a credible case for increasing the budget.
A credible estimate includes clear assumptions.
The company needs a credible plan for reducing emissions.

items.meaning: Logical, clear, and easy to understand as a whole.
items.explanation: Use it when ideas, arguments, or plans connect well and make sense from beginning to end.
items.origin: From Latin cohaerere, meaning to stick together or be connected.
examples: The proposal needs a more coherent structure.
She presented a coherent argument for the new strategy.
The team created a coherent plan across all departments.
His notes were detailed but not yet coherent.
A coherent story helps customers understand the value of the product.

items.meaning: Good at finding clever and effective ways to solve problems.
items.explanation: Use it to describe someone who makes good use of the time, tools, and information available to them.
items.origin: From resource, based on Old French resourse: a source of help or aid.
examples: The resourceful team found a workaround before the deadline.
She was resourceful when the usual supplier was unavailable.
A resourceful manager can solve problems without wasting money.
He gave a resourceful answer using the tools already available.
Their resourceful approach turned a limitation into an advantage.
